# Matplotlib {background-color="#03A062"}

## Figures, axes and artists

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 100)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 2.6))
ax.plot(x, np.sin(x), label="sin")
ax.plot(x, np.cos(x), label="cos")
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_title("A Figure holding one Axes")
ax.legend();
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Figure**: the whole canvas, which you save to a file
- **Axes**: one plot area, with its own x and y axis. A figure can hold many
- **Artists**: everything drawn (lines, text, ticks, legend), each with properties you can change
:::
::::

## `pyplot` versus `fig, ax`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**pyplot style**: acts on the "current" axes

```python
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.xlabel("time (s)")
plt.title("Trial 3")
```

Fine for a quick look at one plot.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Object-oriented style**: says which axes

```python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axes[0].plot(x, y)
axes[0].set_xlabel("time (s)")
axes[1].hist(y)
```

Use it for anything with more than one panel, and in functions. We use this style throughout.
:::
::::

<br>

Most `plt.xlabel(...)` calls become `ax.set_xlabel(...)`. The Matplotlib docs explain [the two interfaces](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/figure/api_interfaces.html).

## Images, colormaps and saving

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
face = plt.imread("data/face.png").mean(axis=2)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5, 2))
axes[0].imshow(face)
axes[1].imshow(face, cmap="gray")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_axis_off()
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- A 2-D array has no colour: `imshow` maps values through a **colormap**
- Use perceptually uniform maps (`viridis`, `gray`); diverging maps (`RdBu_r`) only for data centred on zero
- `origin="lower"` for graphs, the default `"upper"` for images
:::
::::

```python
fig.savefig("figure.pdf")                         # vector: line plots, for papers
fig.savefig("figure.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")  # raster: images, slides
```

# seaborn {background-color="#03A062"}

## Statistical plots from DataFrames

```{python}
#| echo: false
wide = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_all.csv")
gapminder = pd.wide_to_long(
    wide, stubnames=["gdpPercap", "lifeExp", "pop"], i="country", j="year", sep="_"
).reset_index()
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{python}
#| output: false
import seaborn as sns

sns.relplot(
    data=gapminder.query("year == 2007"),
    x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp",
    hue="continent", size="pop",
    sizes=(10, 600),
).set(xscale="log")
```

- Each argument maps a **column** to a visual property
- Legends, colours and sizes come for free
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
g = sns.relplot(
    data=gapminder.query("year == 2007"),
    x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", hue="continent", size="pop",
    sizes=(10, 600), alpha=0.7, height=4, aspect=1.3,
)
g.set(xscale="log", xlabel="GDP per capita (log)", ylabel="Life expectancy")
sns.reset_orig()
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 11})
```
:::
::::

## When to reach for seaborn

| seaborn | plain Matplotlib |
|---|---|
| Data already in a tidy DataFrame: one row per observation | Arrays, images, custom layouts |
| Colour, size or facet by a category | Full control of every artist |
| Aggregates with confidence intervals (`lineplot`, `barplot`) | Unusual plot types |
| Distributions: `histplot`, `kdeplot`, `boxplot`, `violinplot` | Animations, interactive widgets |

<br>

seaborn draws **with** Matplotlib, so `ax=`, `fig.savefig` and everything from the last block still work.

# SciPy {background-color="#03A062"}

## What lives where

| Submodule | For |
|---|---|
| `scipy.optimize` | Fitting (`curve_fit`), minimising, root finding |
| `scipy.stats` | Distributions, statistical tests |
| `scipy.signal` | Filtering, spectra, peak finding |
| `scipy.fft` | Fourier transforms |
| `scipy.ndimage` | N-D image filters, morphology, measurements |
| `interpolate` · `integrate` · `linalg` · `sparse` · `spatial` | … and more |

`import scipy as sp`, then `sp.optimize.curve_fit`, `sp.stats.ttest_ind` and so on.

## Check SciPy before writing your own

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
import scipy as sp

def model(t, amplitude, rate):
    return amplitude * np.exp(-rate * t)

t = np.linspace(0, 5, 40)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
y = model(t, 3.0, 1.2) + rng.normal(0, 0.1, t.size)

params, cov = sp.optimize.curve_fit(model, t, y,
                                    p0=[1, 1])
errors = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))
params.round(2), errors.round(2)
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Tested, documented and fast (usually compiled code underneath)
- Returns uncertainties too: the square root of the covariance's diagonal gives the standard errors
- Search the [API reference](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/) **before** writing a loop
:::
::::

# scikit-image {background-color="#03A062"}

## Images are NumPy arrays

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{python}
import skimage as ski

image = ski.io.imread("data/human_mitosis.png")
print(image.shape, image.dtype)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3, 3))
ax.imshow(image, cmap="gray")
ax.set_axis_off()
```
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
- 2-D grey `(rows, cols)`; colour `(rows, cols, 3)`; stacks add `z` or time axes
- Usually `uint8` (0–255) or `uint16`. Remember yesterday's overflow!
- Most filters return `float` images in [0, 1]
- Everything from NumPy works: slicing crops, masks select, `.mean()` measures
- Human cells stained for DNA, from Moffat *et al.* (2006), CC0
:::
::::

## Filtering and thresholding

```{python}
smoothed = ski.filters.gaussian(image, sigma=1)   # reduce noise
threshold = ski.filters.threshold_otsu(smoothed)  # automatic threshold
binary = smoothed > threshold                     # a boolean mask

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 3))
images = {"original": image, "gaussian": smoothed, "Otsu": binary}
for ax, (title, im) in zip(axes, images.items()):
    ax.imshow(im[:150, :150], cmap="gray")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_axis_off()
```

## Labelling and segmentation

```{python}
cleaned = ski.morphology.remove_small_objects(binary, max_size=30)
cleaned = ski.segmentation.clear_border(cleaned)
labels = ski.measure.label(cleaned)  # 0 = background, 1..N = objects
print("objects found:", labels.max())

overlay = ski.color.label2rgb(labels, image=image, bg_label=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 2.2))
ax.imshow(overlay[180:330, :])
ax.set_axis_off()
```

Touching nuclei merge into one object; a **watershed** separates them (stretch exercise).

## Measuring objects with `regionprops`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{python}
props = ski.measure.regionprops_table(
    labels,
    intensity_image=image,
    properties=["label", "area",
                "eccentricity", "intensity_mean"],
)
nuclei = pd.DataFrame(props)
nuclei.head(4).round(2)
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
- One row per object, ready for pandas and seaborn
- Dozens of properties: `area`, `perimeter`, `centroid`, `bbox`, `orientation`, `intensity_*`, …
- Measurements in **pixels**: multiply by the pixel size for µm
:::
::::

# Whirlwind tour {background-color="#03A062"}

## xarray: labelled N-D arrays

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Problem:** with NumPy you must remember that time is axis 0 and look up indices by hand.

```python
ds = xr.open_dataset("air_temperature_daily.nc")
air = ds["air"]
air.sel(lat=50, lon=260, method="nearest")
air.sel(time="2013-07").mean(dim="time")
air.groupby("time.season").mean()
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Dimensions have **names**; coordinates have **values** (dates, latitudes, µm)
- Select by label, reduce by name, group by season
- Reads and writes netCDF and Zarr, and plots in one line
- Fits imaging too: `(z, channel, y, x)` with physical units
:::
::::

[notebooks/day2_05_xarray.ipynb]{.notebook} · [tutorial.xarray.dev](https://tutorial.xarray.dev)

## dask: bigger than memory, in parallel

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```python
import dask.array as da

# 3.2 GB, in 100 chunks of 32 MB
x = da.random.random((20_000, 20_000),
                     chunks=(2_000, 2_000))

# instant: only builds a task graph
result = ((x - x.mean(axis=0)) ** 2).mean()

# runs the graph, chunk by chunk
result.compute()
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- A dask array is a grid of NumPy **chunks**
- Operations are **lazy**: they build a task graph
- `.compute()` runs it on all cores, using little memory at a time
- `xr.open_dataset(..., chunks={...})` makes xarray use dask
:::
::::

[notebooks/day2_06_dask.ipynb]{.notebook} · [tutorial.dask.org](https://tutorial.dask.org)

## napari: look at your data

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```python
import napari

viewer = napari.Viewer()
viewer.add_image(image, name="nuclei")
viewer.add_labels(labels, name="seg")
```

Edit the labels with the brush or fill tool, then read them back:

```python
edited = viewer.layers["seg"].data
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- An interactive viewer for N-D images and their annotations: labels, points, shapes, tracks
- Sliders for z, time and channels
- Everything is a NumPy array you can read back from the layer
- Opens a **desktop window**: run it on your own laptop
:::
::::

[notebooks/day2_07_napari.ipynb]{.notebook} · [napari.org/stable/tutorials](https://napari.org/stable/tutorials/)

## Also worth knowing

| Package | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **scikit-learn** | Machine learning: classification, clustering, regression, dimensionality reduction ([SPL chapter](https://lectures.scientific-python.org/packages/scikit-learn/index.html), [PDSH ch. 5](https://jakevdp.github.io/PythonDataScienceHandbook/05.02-introducing-scikit-learn.html)) |
| **Zarr** | Chunked, compressed N-D arrays on disk or in the cloud. Pairs with dask, xarray and napari |
| **Polars** | Fast DataFrames with a lazy query engine: an alternative to pandas for large tables |
| **Numba** | Compiles Python loops to machine code with one decorator, `@numba.njit`, for when vectorising is awkward ([SPL, Optimizing code](https://lectures.scientific-python.org/advanced/optimizing/index.html)) |
